chunks: "The body diode is the PN junction between the MOSFET's body and its drain.
In an N-channel device the body is p-type and the drain is n-type, so there's a diode with its anode at the body and its cathode at the drain.
In a discrete power MOSFET the body is shorted to the source, so it looks like a diode from source to drain, anode at the source.
For a PMOS it's flipped: anode at the drain, cathode at the source. It comes from the construction, not from anything added.
In silicon, any time you put n-type next to p-type you get a junction. The consequence is that an off MOSFET only blocks voltage in one direction.
If the drain goes below the source on an NMOS, the diode conducts regardless of the gate. In practice that matters in two ways.
In a half-bridge, during dead time the inductor current freewheels through the body diode with a 0.
7 to 1 volts drop, wasting power, and when the opposite FET turns on the diode has to recover its stored charge, causing a current spike.
So we turn the channel on during that interval, synchronous rectification, so current takes the low-resistance path.
And if I need to block in both directions, like a load switch with a battery, I put two FETs back to back so one body diode always blocks."
